title: Lemma
body_md: Let $X$ be a topological space in which every compact saturated subset has empty interior. Then the Smyth power space $Q(X)$ is open well-filtered.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that in the Smyth power space $Q(X)$, for open sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$,$\mathcal{U}\ll\mathcal{V}$ if and only if $\mathcal{U}=\emptyset$.
	
	Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a nonempty open set. Then there exists an open set $W\neq\emptyset$ such that $\emptyset\neq\Box W\subseteq\mathcal{U}$. Consider $\Phi_W=\{\Box O\mid\ O\in\mathcal{O}(X), W\nsubseteq O\}$.
	
	Claim 1: $\Phi_W$ is an open cover of $Q(X)$.
	
	Assume that $K\in Q(X)$, then $W\nsubseteq K$ because $K$ has an empty interior. Take $w\in W\setminus K$. Since $K$ is saturated, we can choose an open set $O$ such that $K\subseteq O$ and $w\notin O$. Thus $K\in\Box O\in\Phi_W$.
	
	Claim 2: There is no finite subfamily of $\Phi_W$ that can cover $\Box W$.
	
	Given $\{\Box O_1,...,\Box O_m\}$ is a finite subfamily of $\Phi_W$. Then for each $j\in\{1,...,m\}$, take $w_j\in W\setminus O_j$. Let $L=\uparrow_X\{w_1,...,w_m\}\in Q(X)$. Then $L\subseteq W$ because $W$ is an open set. As a result, $L\in\Box W$. But $L\notin\bigcup_{j=1}^m\Box O_j$ due to the fact that $w_j\in L\setminus O_j$.
	
	To conclude, $\mathcal{U}\nll Q(X)$ and then $\mathcal{U}\ll\mathcal{V}$ if and only if $\mathcal{U}=\emptyset$, which is sufficient to show that $Q(X)$ is open well-filtered.

title: Theorem
body_md: The Hofmann-Lawson space $E$ is not an open well-filtered space but its Smyth power space is open well-filtered.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma 3.1, $Q(E)$ is open well-filtered. Now we prove $E$ is not open well-filtered.

For $n\ge 3$, let $N_n=(1-\frac{1}{n}, 1]$ and $b_n=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n}$. Define $H_n=N_n\times[0,b_n)$, $U_n=E\cap H_n$ and $G=E\cap(I\times[0,\frac{1}{2}))$. Clearly, $U_n$ and $G$ are open sets in $E$ for each $n$.

In order to prove that $\{U_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is a $\ll$-filtered family, we define the map $\rho: \mathcal{O}(Y)\to \mathcal{O}(E)$, which sends each $G$ to the intersection $G\cap E$.

Claim 1: $\rho$ is an order-isomorphism between two open set lattices.

We only need to show that for $G, H\in\mathcal{O}(Y)$, $G\cap E\subseteq H\cap E$ implies $G\subseteq H$. Suppose $G\nsubseteq H$, take $(x,t)\in G\setminus H$. Consider $G_x=\{s\in J\mid (x,s)\in G\}$ and $H_x=\{s\in J\mid (x,s)\in H\}$. Note that the map $f$ from $J$ to $I\times J$ which sends each $s$ to $(x,s)$ is continuous and $G_x=f^{-1}(G), H_x=f^{-1}(H)$. Thus they are open sets in $J$ and we can take $g,h\in I$ such that $G_x=[0,g)$ and $H_x=[0,h)$. Since $(x,t)\in G\setminus H, t\in G_x$ but $t\notin H_x$, that is, $h\le t<g$. Therefore, $h<g$. Now consider $x$: If $x\in A$, take $s\in (h,g)\cap\mathbb{Q}$; If $x\in I\setminus A$, take $s\in (h,g)\cap(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})$. No matter what the situation is, we can guarantee that $(x,s)\in E$. But $h<s<g$ implies $s\in G_x\setminus H_x$, whence $(x,s)\in G\setminus H$. To conclude, $G\cap E\nsubseteq H\cap E$, a contradiction.

Claim 2: $H_{n+1}\ll H_n$ for each $n\ge 3$.

This is obvious because $H_{n+1}\subseteq [1-\frac{1}{n+1}, 1]\times [0,b_{n+1}]\subseteq H_n$ and $[1-\frac{1}{n+1}, 1]\times [0,b_{n+1}]$ is compact in $Y$.

Note that $U_n=E\cap H_n$, then $U_{n+1}\ll U_n$ for each $n\ge 3$ by Claims 1 and 2, which implies $\{U_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is a $\ll$-filtered family.

It is evident that $\bigcap_{n\ge 3} U_n=E\cap(\{1\}\times[0,\frac{1}{2}])=\{1\}\times([0,\frac{1}{2})\setminus\mathbb{Q})\subseteq G$, but $U_n\nsubseteq G$ for each $n$ because $A$ is dense and the "height" of $U_n$ is strictly bigger than $\frac{1}{2}$.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $X$ be a locally compact space, $C$ a nonempty compact subset of $X$, and $U$ an open set with $C\subseteq U$. Then there exists $L\in Q(X)$ such that $C\subseteq int_X L\subseteq L\subseteq U$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For every $c\in C$, since $X$ is locally compact, there exists $H_c\in Q(X)$ such that $c\in int_X H_c\subseteq H_c\subseteq U$. Then $\{int_X H_c\}_{c\in C}$ is an open cover of $C$ and $C\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^n int_X H_{c_i}$ because $C$ is compact. Let $L=\bigcup_{i=1}^n H_{c_i}\in Q(X)$ and it is easy to see $C\subseteq int_X L\subseteq L\subseteq U$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: A locally compact space $X$ is $PF$-well-filtered if and only if it is $PF$-sober.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every $PF$-sober space is $PF$-well-filtered.
	
	Conversely, given an irreducible set $\mathcal{A}\subseteq Q(X)$ and define $\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}=\{L\in Q(X) \mid \exists K\in\mathcal{A}, K\subseteq int_X L\}$.
	
	Since $\mathcal{A}\neq\emptyset$, take $K\in\mathcal{A}$. Then by Lemma 3.3, there exists $L\in Q(X)$ such that $K\subseteq int_X L\subseteq\ L\subseteq X$. So $L\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$, which implies $\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}\neq\emptyset$.
	
	Given $L_1, L_2\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$, then $\mathcal{A}\cap\Box(int_X L_i)\neq\emptyset$ for $i=1, 2$. Due to the irreducibility of $\mathcal{A}$, we have $\mathcal{A}\cap\Box(int_X L_1)\cap\Box(int_X L_2)\neq\emptyset$. Take $K_3$ in this intersection and by Lemma 3.3, there exists $L_3\in Q(X)$ such that $K_3\subseteq int_X L_3\subseteq L_3\subseteq int_X L_1\cap int_X L_2$. Thus $L_3\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$ with $L_3\subseteq L_1\cap L_2$. Therefore, $\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is filtered.
	
	Claim: $\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}=\bigcap\mathcal{A}$.
	
	Assume $z\notin\bigcap\mathcal{A}$, then there exists $K\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $z\notin K$. Because $K$ is saturated, $z\notin G$ for some $G\in\mathcal{O}(X)$ and $K\subseteq G$. By Lemma 3.3, there exists $L\in Q(X)$ such that $K\subseteq int_X L\subseteq L\subseteq G$. Hence, $L\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$ and $z\notin L$, which implies $z\notin\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$. To conclude, we have $\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal{A}$. The reverse inclusion is obvious.
	
	Therefore, if $\bigcap\mathcal{A}=\uparrow x\subseteq U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$, then $\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}=\uparrow x\subseteq U$. Since $X$ is $PF$-well-filtered, there exists $L\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}}$ satisfying $L\subseteq U$. Thus there exists $K\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $K\subseteq int_X L\subseteq L\subseteq U$.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $X$ be a $T_0$ space. Then $X$ is $PF$-well-filtered if and only if for each $C\in RD(X)$, $C=C^{ul}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(\Rightarrow)$ For any $C\in RD(X)$. Suppose $C^{ul}\nsubseteq C$, take $x\in C^{ul}\setminus C$. Let $U=X\setminus C$, then $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$ with $x\in U$ and $C^u\subseteq\uparrow x$. Since $C$ is a Rudin set, take $\mathcal{K}$, which witnesses this. For each $K\in\mathcal{K}$, define $L_K$=$\uparrow(C\cap K)$ and $\mathcal{L}=\{L_K\mid K\in\mathcal{K}\}$. It is easy to see that $\mathcal{L}\subseteq Q(X)$ is filtered.
	
	Claim: $\bigcap_{K\in\mathcal{K}} L_K=C^{u}$.
	
	Assume $y\in\bigcap_{K\in\mathcal{K}} L_K$, then for each $K\in\mathcal{K}$, $y\ge c_K$ for some $c_K\in C\cap K$. Consider $B=C\cap\downarrow y$. Obviously, $B$ is closed and $B\subseteq C$ with $c_K\in B\cap K\neq\emptyset$. Thus $C\subseteq\downarrow y$ by the minimality of $C$, which implies $y\in C^u$. The reverse inclusion is obvious.
	
	Now define $\mathcal{M}=\{M_K\mid K\in\mathcal{K}\}$, where $M_K=L_K\cup\uparrow x$. It is evident that $\mathcal{M}\subseteq Q(X)$ is filtered and $\bigcap_{K\in\mathcal{K}} M_K=C^u\cup\uparrow x=\uparrow x\subseteq U$. So $M_{K_0}\subseteq U=X\setminus C$ for some $K_0\in\mathcal{K}$ by the $PF$-well-filteredness of $X$. But $\emptyset\neq C\cap K_0\subseteq L_{K_0}\subseteq M_{K_0}$, which implies $C\cap M_{K_0}\neq\emptyset$, a contradiction.
	
	Note that when $C^u=\emptyset$, we can also show that $\bigcap_{K\in\mathcal{K}} L_K=\emptyset$ and the conclusion still holds.
	
	$(\Leftarrow)$ Let $\mathcal{K}\subseteq Q(X)$ be filtered and $\bigcap\mathcal{K}=\uparrow x\subseteq U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$. Suppose for each $K\in\mathcal{K}$, $K\nsubseteq U$. Set $F=X\setminus U$, it is closed. Thus $K\cap F\neq\emptyset$ implies that there exists set $C$ satisfying the condition of Lemma 3.5. Consequently, $C\in RD(X)$ and $C^u\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal{K}=\uparrow x$ due to the fact that $C\cap K\neq\emptyset$. As a result, $x\in C^{ul}=C$, which implies that $x\in C\subseteq F=X\setminus U$, a contradiction.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{liu2021function}
	Let $X$ and $Y$ be two $T_0$ spaces. Given $y\in Y$, consider the mapping $\xi \colon Y \to [X,Y], \ y \mapsto \xi_y$, where $\xi_y(x)=y$ for all $x\in X$. Then $\xi$ is continuous.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{li2023some}
	Let $X$ be a nonempty $T_0$ space. For each $x\in X$, define a function $F_x: [X,Y]\to Y$ by $F_x(f)=f(x)$ for any $f\in [X,Y]$. Then $F_x$ is continuous.

title: Theorem
body_md: If $X$ is a nonempty $T_0$ space and $[X,Y]$ is a $PF$-well-filtered space, then $Y$ is a $PF$-well-filtered space.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $A\in RD(Y)$, we have $\overline{\xi(A)}\in RD([X,Y])$ by Lemma 4.2. Since $[X,Y]$ is a $PF$-well-filtered space, $\overline{\xi(A)}=\overline{\xi(A)}^{ul}$. 
	
	Claim: For any $y\in A^{ul}$, $\xi_y\in\overline{\xi(A)}^{ul}$.
	
	Assume that $g\in\overline{\xi(A)}^u$, then $\xi(A)\subseteq\overline{\xi(A)}$, which implies $\xi(A)\subseteq\downarrow g$. For each $x\in X$, given $a\in A$, then $\xi_a\le g$. It follows that $a\le g(x)$. Thus $g(x)\in A^u$. So $y\le g(x)$. Therefore, $\xi_y\le g$. We conclude that $\xi_y\in\overline{\xi(A)}^{ul}$.
	
	Hence, $\xi_y\in\overline{\xi(A)}$. Given $x_0\in X$, note that $\xi(A)\subseteq F_{x_0}^{-1}(A)$ and $F_{x_0}$ is continuous, we have $\overline{\xi(A)}\subseteq F_{x_0}^{-1}(A)$; as a result, $y\in A$, which implies $A^{ul}=A$. Consequently, $Y$ is a $PF$-well-filtered space by Proposition 3.6.

title: Theorem
body_md: If $X$ is a nonempty $T_0$ space and $[X,Y]$ is a $PF$-sober space, then $Y$ is a $PF$-sober space.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Take $X=\{a,b\}$ endowed with the discrete topology and $Y=\mathbb{N}$ with the Alexandroff topology under the usual order. It is clear that $X$ is core-compact and $Y$ is $PF$-sober.
	
	Claim 1: The product $Y^2$ is not $PF$-well-filtered.
	
	For each $n\ge 2$, let $K_n=\uparrow(n,1)\cup\uparrow(1,2)$. Obviously, it is a compact saturated set. Thus the filtered intersection $\bigcap_{n\ge 2} K_n=\uparrow(1,2)=\mathbb{N}\times\uparrow2\in\mathcal{O}(Y^2)$, but $K_n\nsubseteq\uparrow(1,2)$ for each $n\ge 2$.
	
	Claim 2: $[X,Y]\cong Y^2$.
	
	Define two maps $\phi$ and $\psi$ as follows:	
	\[
	\phi: [X,Y] \to Y \times Y, \qquad
	\psi: Y \times Y \to [X,Y],
	\]
	where
	\[
	\phi(f)=(f(a),f(b)),
	\]
	and
	\[
	\psi(y_1,y_2)\in [X,Y]
	\]
	satisfies
	\[
	\psi(y_1,y_2)(a)=y_1, \qquad
	\psi(y_1,y_2)(b)=y_2.
	\]
	
	It is evident that $\phi$ and $\psi$ are mutually inverse maps. We only need to prove that both maps are continuous.
	
	Note that $\sigma(\mathcal{O}(X))=\{\emptyset, \mathcal{O}(X), \{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}, \{\{b\},\{a,b\}\}, \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}\}, \{\{a, b\}\}\}.$ Denote $\mathcal{H}_a=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$ and $\mathcal{H}_b=\{\{b\},\{a,b\}\}$. For each $U\in\mathcal{O}(Y)$, 
	
	\begin{align*}
		N(\mathcal{H}_a\leftarrow U) &= \{f: X\to Y\mid f^{-1}(U)\in\mathcal{H}_a\}\\
		&=\{f: X\to Y\mid f(a)\in U\}.
	\end{align*}
	Similarly, $N(\mathcal{H}_b\leftarrow U)=\{f: X\to Y\mid f(b)\in U\}$. Consider $\{U\times V\mid U, V\in\mathcal{O}(Y)\}$, which is a basis for the topology of $Y\times Y$. Note that 
	 
	 \begin{align*}
	 	\phi^{-1}(U\times V) &= \{f: X\to Y\mid f(a)\in U, f(b)\in V\}\\
	 	&= N(\mathcal{H}_a\leftarrow U)\cap N(\mathcal{H}_b\leftarrow V)\in \mathcal{O}([X,Y]).
	 \end{align*}
	 As a result, $\phi$ is continuous.
	
	For any $\mathcal{H}\in\sigma(\mathcal{O}(X))$, $U\in\mathcal{O}(Y)$, 
	\begin{align*}
		N(\mathcal{H}\leftarrow U) &= \{f: X\to Y\mid f^{-1}(U)\in\mathcal{H}\}\\
		&= \{f: X\to Y\mid \exists V\in\mathcal{H} \,\text{such that}\, V\subseteq f^{-1}(U)\}\\
		&=\{f: X\to Y\mid \exists V\in\mathcal{H}, \forall t\in V, f(t)\in U\}\\
		&=\bigcup_{V\in\mathcal{H}}\bigcap_{t\in V} \{f: X\to Y\mid f(t)\in U\}.
	\end{align*}
	It follows that $$\phi(N(\mathcal{H}\leftarrow U))=\bigcup_{V\in\mathcal{H}}\bigcap_{t\in V}\phi(\{f: X\to Y\mid f(t)\in U\}).$$
	Since $V\in\{\emptyset, \{a,b\}, \{a\}, \{b\}\}$,
	
	\[\bigcap_{t\in V}\phi(\{f: X\to Y\mid f(t)\in U\})=\begin{cases}
		Y\times Y, & V=\emptyset\\
		U\times Y, & V=\{a\}\\
		Y\times U, & V=\{b\}\\
		U\times U, & V=\{a,b\},
	\end{cases}\]
	which is open in $Y\times Y$. Thus $\phi(N(\mathcal{H}\leftarrow U))$ is the union of some open sets. Therefore, $$\psi^{-1}(N(\mathcal{H}\leftarrow U))=\phi(N(\mathcal{H}\leftarrow U))\in\mathcal{O}(Y\times Y).$$
	We conclude that $[X,Y]$ is not $PF$-well-filtered. Obviously, it is not a $PF$-sober space.

title: Theorem
body_md: The reflective hull of $PFSOB$ in $TOP_0$ is $TOP_0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to see that $PFSOB$ contains a non-$T_1$ space. Then the reflective hull of $PFSOB$ exists by Lemma 5.2. Let $I=[0,1]$ endowed with the Scott topology under the usual order. It is clear that $I$ is sober; consequently, it is $PF$-sober. For any $T_0$ space $X$, define $Y=I^{\mathcal{O}(X)}$. Then $Y$ is sober and $e: X\to Y$ sends each $x$ to $e(x)$, where 
	
	$$e(x)_U=\begin{cases}
		1, & x\in U\\
		0, & x\notin U
	\end{cases}$$
	for every $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$ is a topological embedding since $e(U)=e(X)\cap\{z\in Y\mid z_U>\frac{1}{2}\}$.
	
	Claim: For each $p\in Y$, $A_p=Y\setminus \{p\}$ endowed with the relative topology from $Y$ is $PF$-sober.
	
	Take $C\in Irr_c(A_p)$, we need to prove that $C_{A_p}^{ul}=C$. Since the inclusion map from $A_p$ to $Y$ is continuous and $Y$ is sober, $\overline{C}^Y=\downarrow_Y q$ for some $q\in Y$. Note that $C$ is closed in $A_p$, thus $C=A_p\cap\downarrow_Y q$. Consider the following three situations:
	
	(1) If $q\neq p$, then $q\in A_p$ and $C=A_p\cap\downarrow_Y q=\downarrow_{A_p}q$ is a cut in $A_p$.
	
	(2) If $q=p=\top$, then $C=A_p\cap\downarrow_Y q=A_p$ is a cut in $A_p$.
	
	(3) If $q=p\neq\top$, take $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$ such that $p_U<1$. Define
	
	 $$(q_n)_V=\begin{cases}
		p_U+\frac{1-p_U}{n+1}, & U=V\\
		p_V, & U\neq V
	\end{cases}$$
	for each $n\ge 1$. Since $q_n>p$, we have $q_n\in A_p$ and $\{q_n\mid n\ge 1\}\subseteq C_{A_p}^u$. It is clear that $\bigcap_{n\ge 1}\downarrow_Y q_n=\downarrow_Y p$. Consequently, $C_{A_p}^{ul}\subseteq\bigcap_{n\ge 1}\downarrow_Y q_n=\downarrow_Y p$. So $C_{A_p}^{ul}\subseteq\downarrow_Y p\cap A_p=\downarrow_Y q\cap A_p=C$, which implies that $C$ is a cut in $A_p$.
	
	Suppose $\mathcal{K}\subseteq TOP_0$ is a reflective category with $PFSOB\subseteq\mathcal{K}$. Given a $T_0$ space $X$ and let $\eta: X\to KX$ be the $K$-reflection. Since $Y\in PFSOB$, there exists a unique continuous map $f: KX\to Y$ such that $f\circ\eta=e$. For each $p\in Y\setminus e(X)$, the map $e_p: X\to A_p$ is a topological embedding, and $A_p\in\mathcal{K}$ by the Claim above. Thus there exists a unique continuous map $f_p: KX\to A_p$ such that $f_p\circ\eta=e_p$. Let $i_p$ be the inclusion from $A_p$ to $Y$. Then $i_p\circ f_p=f$ by the $K$-reflection $\eta$ and the object $Y$. Therefore, $f(KX)\subseteq f_p(KX)\subseteq A_p$ for each $p\in Y\setminus e(X)$, which implies that $f(KX)\subseteq\bigcap_{p\in Y\setminus e(X)} Y\setminus\{p\}=e(X)$. Let $e^{-1}: e(X)\to X$ denote the inverse homeomorphism. Then $r=e^{-1}\circ f: KX\to X$ is continuous. Thus $r\circ\eta=e^{-1}\circ f\circ\eta=e^{-1}\circ e=id_X$. 	Note that $(\eta\circ r)\circ\eta=\eta\circ (r\circ\eta)=\eta$. So $\eta\circ r=id_{KX}$ by the $K$-reflection $\eta$ and the object $KX$. We conclude that $X$ is homeomorphic to $KX$ with the continuous map $r$ and $\eta$. Therefore, $X\in\mathcal{K}$, which implies $\mathcal{K}=TOP_0$.
